prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which trap neutral atoms at a magic wavelength and reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the cleanest case on the list of a new measurement technique changing what can be measured. Katori's magic-wavelength idea cancels the light shift so that thousands of atoms can be interrogated Doppler- and recoil-free, which turns a statistical advantage into an accuracy advantage. Performance has gone from the 1e-15 range to about 1e-18, independently reproduced in several laboratories, with intercontinental comparisons and centimetre-to-millimetre gravitational redshift measurements that are real experimental results rather than projections. The attribution is unusually tidy: Katori originated and first demonstrated the concept, and Ye drove the systematic-uncertainty records, the degenerate-Fermi-gas clock and the comb-clock integration. A two-person prize is therefore faithful to the record. The technique has already enabled other work (constant-variation tests, relativistic geodesy, the roadmap to redefining the second), which is the test I apply when asking whether a field has been opened.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap with prior recognition: 2005 (Hall and Hansch, frequency comb and precision spectroscopy) and 2012 (Wineland and Haroche, control of single quantum systems, including the Al+ ion clock) already honoured the toolbox on which lattice clocks depend, and ion clocks and Lemonde-type fountain work are close relatives. A committee could read this as an incremental advance on an already-rewarded theme. A second reservation is that the formal redefinition of the second has not happened, so the societal payoff is still prospective, and that Takamoto, Hinkley and others who made key early or record demonstrations are outside the credited pair.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth ranks B004 first as a clean atomic-structure idea (magic-wavelength trapping) that yields the most precise measurements ever made and prepares a redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree on the physics and add the experimental angle: the magic-wavelength condition only matters because the control of lattice-induced shifts, blackbody radiation and density effects has been demonstrated at the 1e-18 level in several independent labs. That reproducibility is what separates this from a clever proposal. Where I would push back on us both is the 2005/2012 overlap: atomic structure and laser-stabilisation experts will see continuity with comb and ion-clock work, and we should be able to say precisely what is new, namely many-atom interrogation without Doppler and recoil shifts, rather than assume the answer.

responses.point: Ulf Danielsson ranks B004 only eighth, valuing it as a measurement advance connected to tests of gravity, and puts the baryon acoustic oscillation ruler (B045) and IceCube (B032) first and second as new windows on the dark sector and the universe.
responses.response: I take the point that BAO and IceCube are discoveries about nature while a clock is an instrument, and that is a fair line of attack. But gravitational redshift measured across millimetres in a lattice clock, and the sensitivity to variation of constants and ultralight dark-matter couplings, are exactly the kind of fundamental probes this technique now delivers. BAO is a strong measurement, yet the credited trio is awkward (Sunyaev's role is theoretical and early, the survey teams are large) and I do not see how the committee gets a defensible three-name credit. IceCube I respect, but the credited set drops hundreds of collaborators and Yoshida, which is a harder attribution problem than for the clock pair.

responses.point: Goran Johansson ranks circuit QED (B034) first as a genuinely new regime of strong light-matter coupling on a chip that underlies essentially all superconducting quantum processors, and proposes Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf.
responses.response: I ranked B034 second and share the view that circuit QED opened a field and enabled follow-on work, so I would keep it as my first alternative. My reservation is attribution and timing rather than merit. Dropping Girvin or Blais from a four-name theory-plus-experiment story is hard to justify, and the 2025 prize to Clarke, Devoret and Martinis for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits makes me ask whether the committee wants superconducting-circuit work again so soon. I would also like to see the case that the architecture, as opposed to the later transmon and materials engineering, is the part with decisive priority.

responses.point: Mark Pearce ranks B004 first as a clean, original instrument advance two orders of magnitude beyond caesium fountains, and has IceCube (B032) second as a large new observational window.
responses.response: We agree on the first choice and on the value of instruments that open a new measurement regime. I would qualify the IceCube comparison: the neutrino telescope is a real discovery and a remarkable engineering effort, but the identification of sources (TXS 0506+056, Galactic plane) is a few years old and the credited names do not cover the collaboration. Because the clock case has independent confirmation, long-term comparisons and a settled attribution, I see it as the more mature and the more defensible of the two for this year.

responses.point: Olle Eriksson puts magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B010) first as a theory-predicted, experimentally confirmed new platform for correlated insulators and superconductivity, and sees B004 as exemplary in precision but ranks it sixth.
responses.response: The Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiments is a compelling theory-experiment story and I do not dispute its field-opening nature. My concern is maturity and reproducibility: device-to-device variation in twist angle, strain and disorder is still large, the nature of the superconductivity is unresolved, and the exclusion of Cao, the first author of the decisive experiments, from the credited names troubles me. The clock result is by contrast quantitatively settled, and I would be happy to see B010 return once the physics has stabilised.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 (frequency comb) and 2012 (single quantum systems, ion clocks) prizes.
Whether limiting the credit to Katori and Ye is acceptable given the contributions of Takamoto, Lemonde, Hinkley, Ludlow and others.
How much weight the committee gives to the pending redefinition of the second as evidence of impact.
Whether a two-part prize pairing the clock with a quantum-technology topic (for example circuit QED) is worth the loss of credit coherence.
statement.conflict_note: No personal conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. A mild institutional overlap exists with B034 and other quantum-technology candidates, since I serve on the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology management team, which is Chalmers-led and overlaps with Goran Johansson's home institution and works on superconducting-qubit technology. I also have a company role at Deep Light Vision AB and an atomic-physics and rare-earth quantum-memory background that is adjacent to B004, B036 and B013, though without direct collaboration with any named credited candidate that I know of.
